awd_titl_txt: DDRIG in DRMS: Effects of Social Support on Persuasive Messaging for Preventive Medical Practices
awd_abstract_narration:
This research investigates how to increase the impact of health risk messages in naturalistic settings by considering the social contexts in which messages are received. Many health campaign and intervention messages are based on well-tested theories. Though effective in controlled experiments, communication intervention messages often fall short in real-world contexts. This project tests how adding social support elements, including encouraging messages and information aids, can enhance health message effectiveness, such as increasing people’s confidence in adopting risk mitigation behaviors. Study findings contribute to scientific progress and societal well-being by advancing knowledge in health communication and social support. The research provides insights into designing effective risk communication campaigns and interventions that account for social and contextual factors, offering a blueprint for improving health outcomes in the future. 

The project involves a three-phase intervention. In the first two phases, interviews and focus groups are conducted to guide the development of intervention materials. In the third phase, an online intervention delivers a strategic health video to participants to influence their beliefs and intentions, followed by social support text messages for two weeks. The study provides practical guidance for designing health risk communication campaigns and interventions that are not only scientifically grounded but also responsive to real-life social contexts.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
Persuasive messaging has the potential to influence people’s health awareness, attitudes, beliefs, and behaviors. Previous experimental studies have provided support for the effectiveness of persuasive messages, but the translation of theoretically informed messages into real-world health campaigns and interventions has demonstrated limited effectiveness. One possible explanation for this discrepancy is that message effects do not occur in isolation but are shaped by the social and contextual environments in which individuals receive, interpret, and act upon messages. Thus, this dissertation examined how social support may influence audiences’ responses to strategic health messages in the context of promoting human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination and pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) use among young men who have sex with men (MSM). The development of the strategic messages was guided by the integrative model of behavioral prediction (IMBP), a behavioral theory that has been widely applied to inform the design of health messages and interventions. 

This dissertation involved a three-phase intervention. Phase 1 consisted of interviews with young MSM to explore their beliefs and preferences regarding health promotion, HPV vaccination, PrEP use, social support, and intervention delivery. Findings from these interviews informed the development of promotional health messages, social support components, and the overall intervention logistics. Phase 2 involved focus group evaluations with young MSM and scholars who have expertise in health communication or MSM populations to assess and refine intervention materials, ensuring that the intervention was relatable and appropriate for the target audience. Phase 3 consisted of a two-week intervention in which young MSM participants first viewed an IMBP-based video promoting PrEP and HPV vaccination and subsequently received different types of social support (emotional, informational, or mixed support), as part of the intervention. 

Findings from Phase 1 revealed young MSM’s favorable attitudes toward both PrEP and HPV vaccination, important social referents whose opinions and behaviors may influence their decisions, and key facilitators and barriers related to behavioral adoption. Participants also identified preferences for different types of social support that may address barriers and facilitate behavioral change. Phase 2 resulted in revisions and refinements to draft intervention materials to improve audience relevance, relatability, and clarity. Findings from Phase 3 showed that exposure to the IMBP-based video increased participants’ attitudes, perceived norms, efficacy, and intention to use PrEP, although similar effects were not observed for HPV vaccination. The effects of subsequent social support varied by support type. Specifically, after watching the IMBP-based video, receiving informational support over two weeks was associated with increased positive attitudes toward PrEP and greater efficacy for both PrEP use and HPV vaccination, while receiving mixed support was associated with more favorable attitudes toward PrEP. More importantly, receiving subsequent emotional support was associated with behavioral indicators for both health behaviors: participants who watched the IMBP-based video followed by emotional support were more likely to report actions such as having scheduled a medical appointment or having consulted with a healthcare provider. 

This project contributes to health communication and persuasion research by demonstrating how social support can complement strategic messaging and influence audiences’ responses to health interventions. The findings suggest that future message design theories and interventions should consider not only message characteristics but also the broader social contexts in which audiences and messages are situated. More broadly, this project informs the development of future health interventions by demonstrating the value of an audience-centered, mixed-methods approach and a combination intervention formula: using theory-based messages as an initial component to influence beliefs and intentions, followed by social support strategies to complement messages and facilitate behavioral change.  

The co-PI successfully defended the dissertation at Cornell University and archived the dissertation through ProQuest in 2025 under the supervision of the PI. Three manuscripts resulting from this project have been developed and are currently under review at two behavioral science journals and one communication journal. Findings from this project will also be disseminated through presentations at an HIV conference and a sexual health-related summit in October 2026.
